adds.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's per-state table states that Baja California Sur's congress passed a reform in 2021 modifying the Civil Code to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; in June 2023 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled that it was unconstitutional to exclude children and adolescents from accessing that procedure; and in 2024 the state congress passed a further reform amending the Civil Code and expanding legal gender recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people. This is the jurisdiction-specific legal history the record's summary asserts, with the same reform years and Supreme Court trigger.

adds.title: Baja California Sur reconoce la identidad de género de infancias trans y no binarias – El Financiero
adds.summary: El Financiero reports (Gilberto Santisteban, 27 June 2024) that the Baja California Sur state congress approved a reform to the state Civil Code allowing minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, with administrative processes described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children; the XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court, the June 2023 ruling that had struck down the adult-only limit. This directly corroborates the record's 2024-reform claim for Baja California Sur.

adds.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table states that in 2018 Coahuila's congress passed a law creating the Law on Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, establishing an administrative procedure for the recognition of self-identified gender identity, and links the official gazette text of the reform (arts. 124-128, pp. 20-21). This is the jurisdiction-specific legal fact (law, year, administrative-procedure mechanism) that the record's summary asserts.

adds.title: Permitirán nueva identidad legal por cambio de género - El Heraldo de Saltillo
adds.summary: El Heraldo de Saltillo reports (13 November 2018) that proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira shaped the new Ley del Registro Civil del Estado presented to the plenary of the Coahuila congress, which proposes the legal recognition of trans people under their new legal personality; the dictamen, approved by unanimity, reforms article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and creates the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction. This is a dated, outcome-specific local-news account of the 2018 law the record cites as 'among the earlier such enactments in Mexico'.

adds.title: En Coahuila, alrededor de mil 500 personas han formalizado su cambio de identidad de género - El Heraldo de Saltillo
adds.summary: El Heraldo de Saltillo reports (31 March 2023) that Coahuila's Civil Registry director, Ricardo Malacara, said that from early 2019 to March 2023 around 1,500 people in Coahuila had completed the legal gender-identity change procedure before the Civil Registry, in both directions (male to female and female to male), and that approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in the state. This is the only region-specific implementation-outcome data found for Coahuila and shows the administrative procedure the record describes is functioning at scale.

adds.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table states, under Querétaro, that the state has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people (as of the March 2025 map, which counts 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated). This is the jurisdiction-specific basis for the record's statement that Querétaro is one of six states HRW lists as never having legislated any legal-gender-recognition procedure.

adds.title: Terapias de conversión: Pese a ley aprobada, hay más pendientes legislativos para comunidad LGBT+ - Tribuna de Querétaro
adds.summary: Tribuna de Querétaro reports (20 September 2023, with Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación spokesman Walter López) that the reform to Querétaro's Penal Code prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called 'conversion therapies', was published and is in force; it sets a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture; the group calls it a milestone compared with states where the ban remains unpublished but says a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending. This corroborates the record's claim that Querétaro's congress banned conversion practices with 2-6 year penalties, sourced to a Querétaro outlet.
